analysis.one_liner: Caps pay for executives of taxpayer-bailed-out banks at the President's salary.
analysis.headline: A bill to cap pay for executives at banks receiving federal bailout money died in committee without a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2008 financial crisis, the government was handing out $700 billion to rescue banks under TARP. This bill would have amended that bailout law to bar any employee or executive of a bank receiving bailout money from earning more than the President's salary — about $400,000 — in any form, including bonuses and stock. Banks that wanted to keep paying more would have had to immediately repay every federal dollar they had received, with the money redirected to foreclosure relief.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who funded the bank rescues. The bill would have stopped bailout recipients from paying executives multimillion-dollar packages with money that came from the public, and any bank that refused the cap would have had to pay back the federal funds, which would then go toward helping people facing foreclosure.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any employee or executive of a bank receiving TARP assistance from receiving aggregate annual compensation above the President's salary, in any form — including bonuses, deferred compensation, stock options, and securities.

Counts pay already received before the bailout against the cap: an executive who had already exceeded the President's salary for the year would be prohibited from receiving any further compensation for that year.
A bank that chose not to comply would have to immediately repay every dollar of TARP money it had received, and those repaid funds would be used for foreclosure mitigation efforts.

analysis.who_pays: Executives and highly paid employees of banks taking federal rescue money, who would see pay capped at roughly $400,000 — and the banks themselves, which would lose the ability to recruit with large bonuses while holding federal funds, or have to give the federal money back.

drawbacks.text: A hard pay cap covering all employees — not just top executives — of every assisted institution could make it harder for banks the government already had a stake in to retain staff, a concern supporters of looser pay limits raised during the crisis.

Banks could escape the cap by repaying their TARP money, so the restriction would only bind firms that stayed on federal support; it would not touch compensation at banks that never took bailout funds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea was straightforward: if taxpayers are keeping a bank alive, the bank should not pay its executives more than the President until the money is repaid. The main cost is the practical one that salary caps can push top staff out of firms the government was trying to stabilize. The bill softened that by giving banks an exit — repay the funds — which redirected any returned money to homeowners facing foreclosure. The tradeoff favored taxpayers, but the bill never advanced far enough for those design questions to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced in November 2008 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on November 19, 2008, weeks after the $700 billion bailout law passed, with Sens. Blanche Lincoln and Barbara Boxer as cosponsors.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; the action history shows no further committee or floor action for the remainder of the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009.
The Senate never voted on the bill, and it died when the 110th Congress expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and shareholders of banks receiving TARP money came out ahead: no pay cap was ever imposed, and bailout firms remained free to pay large bonuses and compensation packages with federal support. Taxpayers lost the opportunity to attach that condition to the rescue money.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop the Greed on Wall Street Act on November 19, 2008, capping compensation at TARP-assisted institutions at the President's salary.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 19, 2008 and took no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate leadership of the 110th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote at any point during its two-month life.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call ever occurred, so the party split can't be measured; the bill's three sponsors sat with the Democratic caucus, and the Democratic-led Banking Committee was where the bill stalled.

industries.industry: Large banks and financial firms receiving TARP bailout funds
industries.note: The bill would have capped total pay at roughly the President's salary for every employee of a bailed-out bank, or forced the bank to repay the federal money. These firms received hundreds of billions in public rescue funds while continuing to pay large bonuses, so the bill's interest ran directly against theirs.
